stories.title: Romania shuts nuclear plant, Hungary dams dry Danube River
stories.summary: Romania has shut down its only nuclear plant in a rare move prompted by the lack of cooling water from the Danube River. Hungary, meanwhile, is racing to dam the Danube, trying to keep its Paks plant online.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ImuD The Cernavoda nuclear plant gathers all its cooling water from the Danube Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance Advertisement Romania shut down its lone nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare move amid the drought that has caused record lows on the Danube River and other major waterways in Europe . The Danube is the sole source of cooling water for the Cernavoda plant, which usually generates around one-fifth of Romania's electricity. The power station has only been shut down once before, in 2023, again as a result of drought and a hot summer . Meanwhile, Hungary was scrambling to dam the Danube, as it tries to keep its Paks nuclear power plant at least running at the minimal levels that it has maintained in recent days, which are far below capacity. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations , it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin . The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state , its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore. But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.
